newsitem.title: BARBADOS: Caribbean seeks trade progress in Clinton meeting.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean seeks trade progress in Clinton meeting.

text.p: Caribbean leaders will press U.S. President Bill Clinton for progress in boosting trade at a May 10 meeting on this tiny island, while Clinton will seek to address drug-trafficking and money-laundering issues, officials say.

A draft of the final 42-page document to be signed on May 10, made available to Reuters, recognises the "inextricable link between trade, economic development, security and prosperity" in the Caribbean.

Clinton began his first trip to Latin America on May 5, travelling to Mexico and then on to Costa Rica for a meeting of Central American heads of state. He is scheduled to arrive in Barbados on May 9.
Leaders of the 14-member Caribbean Community (Caricom) say that without progress on trade, economic difficulties can only make the drug trade stronger in the region.
They are particularly concerned about the United States' successful challenge to a European Union banana regime which favours Caribbean nations.
Bananas account for 90 percent of export earnings in St. Lucia, 65 percent in St. Vincent and Dominica, and a substantial portion of the earnings of Grenada, Jamaica and Surinam.
The World Trade Organisation has found the EU regime discriminates against bananas exported by U.S. firms operating in Latin America. The ruling has made the region deeply suspicious of Washington.

"We have made every effort to communicate the deleterious effects the WTO ruling would have, even on non-producing states, should it bring the (EU) regime to an abrupt end," said Jamaica's Prime Minister P.J. Patterson, who will chair the summit. "We think (the summit will) have to find other means by which continuing access can be assured" for Caribbean banana exports.

Four years of lobbying have also failed to get the United States to give a range of Caribbean exports, chiefly garments, the same tariff treatment as Mexico receives under the North American Free Trade Agreement.
The World Bank estimates the region could lose a third of its $12.5 billion in annual garment export receipts if the issue is not addressed.
U.S. aid levels to the region have fallen 60 percent in the past decade, a drop of $700 million, Patterson said.
"The United States doesn't seem to understand that if you destroy these economies, they'll just become another Colombia," a senior European diplomat based in Kingston said.

Guyana's late ex-President Cheddi Jagan said last year if the Caribbean economies were wrecked, "people will have to produce marijuana and ship it north ... and not only marijuana, we'll be sending refugees."
U.S. officials estimate 40 percent of all U.S.-bound cocaine is now routed through the region, four times more than 10 years ago.
The United States enjoys a $1.4 billion trade surplus with the region, surpassing its surplus with some major industrialised countries such as France.

Clinton's special envoy to the Americas Thomas "Mack" McLarty said last month in preparatory meetings for the summit that Washington was prepared to work to increase trade opportunities for the Caribbean.
He offered no new money to boost existing aid flows, but said the United States would be willing to back a regional request for development aid from the Inter-American Development Bank.
